---
title: 1 - Setup
---

1. Install required software
If you don't have the required software installed already, start with those:
- A code editing software
- Node.js (14 or higher): https://nodejs.org/en
- Git: https://github.com/git-guides/install-git (note: you may install Git via Visual Studio Code, too)

This tutorial has been created with Visual Studio Code, and the latest versions of Node and Git. Screenshots from Visual Studio Code contain elements that most code editing software have, they may just be in different places or look a bit different (such as Terminal and opening folders). 

2. Create working folder
Create an empty working folder called "webmap" (or anything you like) on your device or cloud, e.g. C:\Users\OneDrive\webmap or C:\Users\your-account\webmap

Open that folder in your code editing software. In VS Code File --> Open Folder... --> Navigate to your \webmap folder, and open it in the software.

[Image of opening folder in VS Code]


2. OpenLayers Quick start

Follow [OpenLayers Quick Start guide](https://openlayers.org/doc/quickstart.html) to initiate your webmap directory inside your working folder. 

For running the npm commands, you need to open a Terminal. In VS Code, a terminal that runs commands inside your working webmap folder is opened via Terminal --> New Terminal

Once hitting the command npm start, you'll be given an url (server that runs the webmap on your local device) where you can view the webmap while you develop it. This is just a local serving of the webmap, and you can view it only locally on your device. 

[Image of terminal opening in VS Code]


3. Explore the basic file structue

The main files you will be working with in this tutorial are main.js, index.html and style.css. Each of these already contain some code, so you won't have to start from complete scratch. Open the local server URL to see how the webmap looks now. Just an OpenStreetMap base map of the world. 

You can also view the webmap by opening the index.html file in your browser. However, you will most likely encounter a bunch of blocked OSM tiles with a warning. This is due to OSM server usage policies to prevent exessive usage of their volunteer-run servers. The OSM tiles will be visible when publishing the webmap, but a bit annoying to look at them in the development stage. Thus, using a local server is recommended to avoid the warnings and actually display the webmap. Read more about OSM policies: [the link to the osm wiki blocked].
